claim: Pharmacological inhibition of ASIC1a reduces neurotoxicity and stroke infarct volumes.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of ASIC1a reduces neurotoxicity and stroke infarct volumes, with the cysteine knot toxin psalmotoxin-1 (PcTx1) being one of the most potent and selective inhibitors.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a known finding.

claim: PcTx1 is one of the most potent and selective inhibitors of ASIC1a.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of ASIC1a reduces neurotoxicity and stroke infarct volumes, with the cysteine knot toxin psalmotoxin-1 (PcTx1) being one of the most potent and selective inhibitors.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a known finding.

claim: PcTx1 binds at the subunit interface in the extracellular domain (ECD) of ASIC1a.
source: PcTx1 binds at the subunit interface in the extracellular domain (ECD), but the mechanism and conformational consequences of the interaction, as well as the number of toxin molecules required for inhibition, remain unknown.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a known finding.

claim: PcTx1 has at least two additional binding modes that are decoupled from the pore besides the known inhibitory binding mode.
source: Besides the known inhibitory binding mode, we propose PcTx1 to have at least two additional binding modes that are decoupled from the pore.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental findings from voltage-clamp fluorometry experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: One of the PcTx1 binding modes induces a long-lived ECD conformation that reduces the activity of an endogenous neuropeptide.
source: One of these modes induces a long-lived ECD conformation that reduces the activity of an endogenous neuropeptide.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing reduced BigDyn activity after PcTx1 exposure.

claim: The long-lived conformational state induced by PcTx1 is proton-dependent.
source: This long-lived conformational state is proton-dependent and can be destabilized by a mutation that decreases PcTx1 sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing pH-dependent fluorescence changes.

claim: The long-lived conformational state induced by PcTx1 can be destabilized by the F350L mutation that decreases PcTx1 sensitivity.
source: This long-lived conformational state is proton-dependent and can be destabilized by a mutation that decreases PcTx1 sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data comparing WT and F350L mutant channels.

claim: Disruption of a single PcTx1 binding site is sufficient to destabilize the toxin-induced conformation.
source: Lastly, the use of concatemeric channel constructs reveals that disruption of a single PcTx1 binding site is sufficient to destabilize the toxin-induced conformation, while functional inhibition is not impaired until two or more binding sites are mutated.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from concatemeric constructs with varying numbers of F350L mutations.

claim: Functional inhibition by PcTx1 is not impaired until two or more binding sites are mutated.
source: Lastly, the use of concatemeric channel constructs reveals that disruption of a single PcTx1 binding site is sufficient to destabilize the toxin-induced conformation, while functional inhibition is not impaired until two or more binding sites are mutated.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from concatemeric constructs showing functional inhibition profiles.

claim: The extracellular domains (ECDs) of ASICs sense pH changes, allowing cations to permeate through the channel pore comprised by the transmembrane domain (TMD).
source: The extracellular domains (ECDs) of ASICs sense pH changes, allowing cations to permeate through the channel pore comprised by the transmembrane domain (TMD) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about ASIC structure and function.

claim: pH-activated current in ASICs underlies fast synaptic transmission.
source: Research over the last two decades has shown that this pH-activated current underlies various physiological processes, such as fast synaptic transmission (Du et al., 2014) and learning and memory (Wemmie et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Du et al., 2014.

claim: pH-activated current in ASICs underlies learning and memory.
source: Research over the last two decades has shown that this pH-activated current underlies various physiological processes, such as fast synaptic transmission (Du et al., 2014) and learning and memory (Wemmie et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wemmie et al., 2002.

claim: Peptide-induced ASIC1a inhibition exhibits neuroprotective effects.
source: Due to recent reports of peptide-induced ASIC1a inhibition exhibiting neuroprotective effects, these trimeric channels have emerged as a potential drug target in neurological diseases, including protection from acidosis-induced neurotoxicity and reduction of infarct volume in mouse models of ischemic stroke (Xiong et al., 2004; Wemmie et al., 2013; Chassagnon et al., 2017; Qiang et al., 2018; Gründer, 2020; Heusser and Pless, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ASIC1a inhibition provides protection from acidosis-induced neurotoxicity in mouse models.
source: Due to recent reports of peptide-induced ASIC1a inhibition exhibiting neuroprotective effects, these trimeric channels have emerged as a potential drug target in neurological diseases, including protection from acidosis-induced neurotoxicity and reduction of infarct volume in mouse models of ischemic stroke (Xiong et al., 2004; Wemmie et al., 2013; Chassagnon et al., 2017; Qiang et al., 2018; Gründer, 2020; Heusser and Pless, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ASIC1a inhibition reduces infarct volume in mouse models of ischemic stroke.
source: Due to recent reports of peptide-induced ASIC1a inhibition exhibiting neuroprotective effects, these trimeric channels have emerged as a potential drug target in neurological diseases, including protection from acidosis-induced neurotoxicity and reduction of infarct volume in mouse models of ischemic stroke (Xiong et al., 2004; Wemmie et al., 2013; Chassagnon et al., 2017; Qiang et al., 2018; Gründer, 2020; Heusser and Pless, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: 30 nM of PcTx1 led to potent alkaline shifts in both the activation curve (ΔpH50_Act > 0.5 pH units at pH 7.9) of ASIC1a WT.
source: In line with previous findings, 30 nM of PcTx1 led to potent alkaline shifts in both the activation curve (ΔpH50_Act > 0.5 pH units at pH 7.9; Figure 1B and D, Supplementary file 1a) and SSD of ASIC1a WT expressed in Xenopus laevis oocytes (ΔpH50_SSD ≈ 0.4 pH units; Figure 1C and D, Supplementary file 1a; Escoubas et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and D and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: 30 nM of PcTx1 led to alkaline shifts in SSD of ASIC1a WT (ΔpH50_SSD ≈ 0.4 pH units).
source: In line with previous findings, 30 nM of PcTx1 led to potent alkaline shifts in both the activation curve (ΔpH50_Act > 0.5 pH units at pH 7.9; Figure 1B and D, Supplementary file 1a) and SSD of ASIC1a WT expressed in Xenopus laevis oocytes (ΔpH50_SSD ≈ 0.4 pH units; Figure 1C and D, Supplementary file 1a; Escoubas et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Labeling of K105C and V80C positions with Alexa Fluor 488 dye reliably reports on conformational changes related to channel gating and modulation by peptides.
source: To this end, we introduced a cysteine residue into the mASIC1a ECD at amino acid position 80 or 105 (Figure 1A) as labeling of these positions with the environmentally sensitive Alexa Fluor 488 dye reliably reports on conformational changes related to channel gating and modulation by peptides (Bonifacio et al., 2014; Borg et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bonifacio et al., 2014 and Borg et al., 2020.

claim: Application of pH 5.5 to K105C* resulted in an inward current and a simultaneous upward deflection of the fluorescence signal.
source: For Alexa Fluor 488-labeled K105C mASIC1a (K105C*), application of pH 5.5 resulted in an inward current and a simultaneous upward deflection of the fluorescence signal (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The fluorescence signal of K105C* typically displayed a transient peak followed by a sustained plateau with a pH dependence similar to pH50_SSD.
source: The latter typically displayed a transient peak, which likely reflects a short-lived open state, followed by a sustained plateau with a pH dependence that was similar to the pH50_SSD, and thus likely reveals a transition related to a desensitized state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1b; note that pH changes between 7.4 and 9.0 did not lead to any fluorescence changes Borg et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Application of 300 nM PcTx1 at pH 7.4 to K105C* resulted in slow upward deflection of the fluorescence.
source: Application of 300 nM PcTx1 at pH 7.4 resulted in slow upward deflection of the fluorescence (Figure 1E, Supplementary file 1c), reminiscent of application of pH 7.0, which led to a similar functional inhibition of channel currents (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: The PcTx1-induced fluorescence signal of K105C* displayed only a modest decrease after 3 min washout with pH 7.4.
source: However, and in stark contrast to the pH 7.0 application, the PcTx1-induced fluorescence signal displayed only a modest decrease after 3 min washout with pH 7.4.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations comparing PcTx1 and pH 7.0 washout.

claim: Post-PcTx1 exposure to pH 8.4 led to an immediate return of fluorescence to baseline level in K105C*.
source: Post-PcTx1 exposure to pH 8.4 led to an immediate return of fluorescence to baseline level; yet, the fluorescence increased as soon as the pH was switched back to 7.4, suggesting the presence of a conformational change that is sustained at pH 7.4 (Figure 1E, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The fluorescence of K105C* increased when pH was switched back to 7.4 after pH 8.4 exposure following PcTx1 treatment.
source: Post-PcTx1 exposure to pH 8.4 led to an immediate return of fluorescence to baseline level; yet, the fluorescence increased as soon as the pH was switched back to 7.4, suggesting the presence of a conformational change that is sustained at pH 7.4 (Figure 1E, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: V80C* showed inverted direction of fluorescence signals upon activation, desensitization, and PcTx1 application compared to K105C*.
source: Here, the direction of the fluorescence signals upon activation, desensitization, and application and washout of 300 nM PcTx1 at 0.3 pH units more alkaline than the pH50_fluorescence of V80C* were inverted (Figure 1G), but resulted in qualitatively similar effects as observed for K105C* (Figure 1E–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D, Supplementary file 1c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: PcTx1 binding induces a long-lived conformational change in the ASIC1a ECD.
source: We conclude that PcTx1 binding induces a long-lived conformational change and that this conformational alteration is not necessarily coupled to the channel pore.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from K105C* and V80C* showing persistent fluorescence changes.

claim: The PcTx1-induced conformational alteration is not necessarily coupled to the channel pore.
source: We conclude that PcTx1 binding induces a long-lived conformational change and that this conformational alteration is not necessarily coupled to the channel pore.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing decoupling between fluorescence and current recovery.

claim: Repeated exposure to pH 5.5 after PcTx1 treatment led to gradual recovery of current amplitude while fluorescence signal remained unchanged.
source: We found that once the channel is in this 'Global' state, repeated exposure to pH 5.5 led to a gradual recovery of the current amplitude, while the fluorescence signal remained effectively unchanged (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Functional recovery from PcTx1 inhibition was dependent on washout time, but not activation.
source: Functional recovery from inhibition was dependent on washout time, but not activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B, Supplementary file 1e), in line with previous observations of tight PcTx1 binding to the open state (Chen et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B and Supplementary file 1e.

claim: PcTx1 binds tightly to the open state of ASIC1a.
source: Functional recovery from inhibition was dependent on washout time, but not activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B, Supplementary file 1e), in line with previous observations of tight PcTx1 binding to the open state (Chen et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2006.

claim: When BigDyn (1 µM) is applied to the PcTx1-induced 'ECDonly' state, the neuropeptide has a much less pronounced effect on the fluorescence signal than without PcTx1 pre-exposure.
source: Strikingly, we found that when BigDyn (1 µM) is applied to the PcTx1-induced 'ECDonly' state, the neuropeptide has a much less pronounced effect on the fluorescence signal than without PcTx1 pre-exposure (Figure 2E and F, Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F and Supplementary file 1g.

claim: Reapplication of PcTx1 to the 'ECDonly' state evoked a similar inhibitory and fluorescence response as the initial application.
source: Conversely, reapplication of PcTx1 to the 'ECDonly' state evoked a similar inhibitory and fluorescence response as the initial application (Figure 2G and H, Supplementary file 1g), indicating that a transition from the 'ECDonly' to the 'Global' state is possible.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H and Supplementary file 1g.

claim: The F350L mutation reduced the pH sensitivity of activation and SSD in ASIC1a.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Sherwood et al., 2009), introducing the F350L mutation reduced the pH sensitivity of activation and SSD, and the presence of 30 nM PcTx1 only led to a slight shift in pH50_SSD, with no discernible effect on channel activation (Figure 3B and C, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: The presence of 30 nM PcTx1 only led to a slight shift in pH50_SSD in F350L mutant, with no discernible effect on channel activation.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Sherwood et al., 2009), introducing the F350L mutation reduced the pH sensitivity of activation and SSD, and the presence of 30 nM PcTx1 only led to a slight shift in pH50_SSD, with no discernible effect on channel activation (Figure 3B and C, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: The inhibitory effect of PcTx1 under physiological pH (7.4) was concentration dependent but dramatically decreased in the F350L variant compared to WT (IC50 ~ 1 µM for F350L compared to ~1 nM for WT).
source: The inhibitory effect of PcTx1 under physiological pH (7.4) was still concentration dependent but dramatically decreased in the F350L variant compared to WT (IC50 ~ 1 µM for F350L compared to ~1 nM for WT; Figure 3D and E, Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E and Supplementary file 1h.

claim: Application of 300 nM PcTx1 to K105C*F350L at pH 7.4 did not elicit any fluorescence changes.
source: In contrast to the K105C* variant, we found that application of 300 nM PcTx1 to K105C*F350L at pH 7.4 did not elicit any fluorescence changes (Figure 3F, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: The fluorescence response curve of the K105C*F350L variant is about 0.1 pH units shifted towards more acidic pH compared to K105C*.
source: Notably, the fluorescence response curve of the K105C*F350L variant is about 0.1 pH units shifted towards more acidic pH compared to K105C* (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: PcTx1 applied at pH 7.3 to K105C*F350L induced a similar slow-onset fluorescence signal as seen for K105C*, albeit slightly less pronounced.
source: Taking this change into account, we applied PcTx1 at pH 7.3. Under these conditions, PcTx1 induced a similar slow-onset fluorescence signal as seen for K105C*, albeit slightly less pronounced, while the functional insensitivity of the F350L variant to PcTx1 remained (Figure 3G, Supplementary file 1c), indicating that the channel can still enter the 'ECDonly' state while the 'Global' binding mode is unfavorable.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: The fluorescence signal of K105C*F350L readily returned to a level indicative of a closed apo state in the first 1–2 min of pH 7.4 washout.
source: A striking difference was apparent in the washout: unlike in K105C*, the fluorescence signal of K105C*F350L readily returned to a level indicative of a closed apo state in the first 1–2 min of pH 7.4 washout, suggesting that the longevity of the 'ECDonly' state is destabilized (Figure 3G, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and Supplementary file 1d.

claim: The functional PcTx1 insensitivity of the F350L variant primarily originates from a destabilization of the PcTx1-induced conformational states ('Global' and 'ECDonly') rather than solely from impaired binding.
source: Together, these data suggest that the functional PcTx1 insensitivity of the F350L variant primarily originates from a destabilization of the PcTx1-induced conformational states ('Global' and 'ECDonly') rather than solely from impaired binding.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing fluorescence changes in F350L mutants.

claim: The pH dependence of the WT/WT/WT and the F350L/F350L/F350L concatemer constructs showed similar pH sensitivities compared to homotrimeric WT and F350L, respectively.
source: The pH dependence of the WT/WT/WT and the F350L/F350L/F350L concatemer constructs showed similar pH sensitivities compared to homotrimeric WT and F350L, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 1i.

claim: The number of F350L subunits determined the pH dependence of concatemeric ASIC1a constructs but was not dependent on the relative positioning of the mutation within the concatemeric ASIC1a construct.
source: The number of F350L subunits determined the pH dependence of concatemeric ASIC1a constructs but was not dependent on the relative positioning of the mutation within the concatemeric ASIC1a construct (Figure 4B–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, and Supplementary file 1i.

claim: For the WT/WT/WT concatemer, pH 5.6-induced currents were inhibited by PcTx1 with an apparent IC50 of around 6 nM at pH 7.4.
source: For the WT/WT/WT concatemer, pH 5.6-induced currents were inhibited by PcTx1 with an apparent IC50 of around 6 nM at pH 7.4 compared to an IC50 of 0.6 nM for WT ASIC1a (Figure 3E, Figure 4F and G, Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and G and Supplementary file 1h.

claim: For the F350L/F350L/F350L concatemer, PcTx1 inhibited pH 5.6-induced currents with an apparent IC50 of around 800 nM.
source: For the F350L/F350L/F350L concatemer, PcTx1 inhibited pH 5.6-induced currents with an apparent IC50 of around 800 nM, similar to the trimeric F350L ASIC1a mutant (Figure 3E, Figure 4F and G, Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and G and Supplementary file 1h.

claim: For concatenated constructs containing two F350L-bearing subunits (WT/F350L/F350L), pH 5.6-induced currents were inhibited by PcTx1 with an apparent IC50 around 100 nM.
source: For concatenated constructs containing two F350L-bearing subunits (WT/F350L/F350L), pH 5.6-induced currents were inhibited by PcTx1 with an apparent IC50 around 100 nM (Figure 4F and G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, and Supplementary file 1h.

claim: The concatemer with only a single F350L-containing subunit (WT/F350L/WT) closely matched the PcTx1 inhibition profile observed for the WT/WT/WT concatemer.
source: Remarkably, the concatemer with only a single F350L-containing subunit (WT/F350L/WT) closely matched the PcTx1 inhibition profile observed for the WT/WT/WT concatemer (Figure 4F and G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, and Supplementary file 1h.

claim: Two WT subunits per mASIC1a trimer are sufficient to observe WT-like functional inhibition by PcTx1.
source: We conclude that two WT subunits per mASIC1a trimer are sufficient to observe WT-like functional inhibition by PcTx1.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from concatemeric constructs showing functional inhibition profiles.

claim: In the WT*/WT*/WT* concatemer, PcTx1 functionally inhibited channel activation and led to the characteristic increase in fluorescence maintained even after removal of PcTx1 from the buffer.
source: In the WT*/WT*/WT* concatemer, PcTx1 functionally inhibited channel activation and led to the characteristic increase in fluorescence maintained even after removal of PcTx1 from the buffer, and this was comparable to what we observed in the K105C* trimer (Figure 1E, Figure 5A, D, and E, Supplementary file 1c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, D, and E and Supplementary file 1c and d.

claim: In WT*/F350L*/WT* concatemers, PcTx1 still had an inhibitory effect on activation and produced a robust fluorescence response.
source: In WT*/F350L*/WT*concatemers, PcTx1 still had an inhibitory effect on activation, in line with the results from nonlabeled constructs, and produced a robust fluorescence response (Figure 5B and D, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and D and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: In WT*/F350L*/WT* concatemers, a marked gradual decrease of the fluorescence signal during the 3 min washout at pH 7.4 was noticeable.
source: In this construct, a marked gradual decrease of the fluorescence signal during the 3 min washout at pH 7.4 was noticeable (Figure 5B and E, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and E and Supplementary file 1d.

claim: In constructs with two F350L-containing subunits, the response of the fluorescence signal to PcTx1 was further reduced, and the fluorescence signal returned to baseline levels in the first 1–2 min of the pH 7.4 washout.
source: In constructs with two F350L-containing subunits, the response of the fluorescence signal to PcTx1 was further reduced, and the fluorescence signal returned to baseline levels (indicative of a closed apo state) in the first 1–2 min of the pH 7.4 washout (Figure 5C–E, Supplementary file 1c and d), reminiscent of the PcTx1 effect on the non-concatemeric K105C*/F350L channel (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C–E and Supplementary file 1c and d.

claim: The presence of a single F350L-containing subunit is sufficient to destabilize the 'ECDonly' state introduced by PcTx1.
source: In summary, our VCF experiments demonstrate that in contrast to the functional modulation the presence of a single F350L-containing subunit is sufficient to destabilize the 'ECDonly' state introduced by PcTx1, further emphasizing that PcTx1 can elicit distinct responses in the ECD and the pore of ASIC1a (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from concatemeric constructs with varying numbers of F350L mutations.

claim: PcTx1 can elicit distinct responses in the ECD and the pore of ASIC1a.
source: In summary, our VCF experiments demonstrate that in contrast to the functional modulation the presence of a single F350L-containing subunit is sufficient to destabilize the 'ECDonly' state introduced by PcTx1, further emphasizing that PcTx1 can elicit distinct responses in the ECD and the pore of ASIC1a (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing decoupling between ECD conformational changes and pore function.

claim: Interfering with a single PcTx1 binding site is sufficient to alter the stability of the ECD conformation.
source: Together, the proposed binding modes emphasize that the conformational changes of the ECD are partially decoupled from the TMD: interfering with a single PcTx1 binding site is sufficient to alter the stability of the ECD conformation, while the pore (or the coupling to it) translates to closed channels only if two or more PcTx1 binding sites are intact (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from concatemeric constructs.

claim: The pore translates to closed channels only if two or more PcTx1 binding sites are intact.
source: Together, the proposed binding modes emphasize that the conformational changes of the ECD are partially decoupled from the TMD: interfering with a single PcTx1 binding site is sufficient to alter the stability of the ECD conformation, while the pore (or the coupling to it) translates to closed channels only if two or more PcTx1 binding sites are intact (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from concatemeric constructs.

claim: PcTx1 is a 40-residue cysteine knot peptide toxin extracted from tarantula venom.
source: Psalmotoxin-1 (PcTx1) is a 40-residue cysteine knot peptide toxin extracted from tarantula venom (Escoubas et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Escoubas et al., 2000.

claim: PcTx1 acts as a potent gating modifier on most ASIC1a-containing channels.
source: It acts as a potent gating modifier on most ASIC1a-containing channels (Chen et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2006) and shifts activation and SSD curves to more alkaline values, thereby effectively inhibiting the channel in the low nanomolar range at neutral pH (Cristofori-Armstrong and Rash, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2005 and Chen et al., 2006.

claim: PcTx1 shifts activation and SSD curves to more alkaline values, thereby effectively inhibiting the channel in the low nanomolar range at neutral pH.
source: It acts as a potent gating modifier on most ASIC1a-containing channels (Chen et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2006) and shifts activation and SSD curves to more alkaline values, thereby effectively inhibiting the channel in the low nanomolar range at neutral pH (Cristofori-Armstrong and Rash, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cristofori-Armstrong and Rash, 2017.

claim: Structural studies have shown that PcTx1 binds to the subunit interfaces of cASIC1, forming contact points with the primary and complementary side of the acidic pocket.
source: Structural studies have shown that PcTx1 binds to the subunit interfaces of cASIC1, forming contact points with the primary and complementary side of the acidic pocket (Dawson et al., 2012; Baconguis et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dawson et al., 2012 and Baconguis et al., 2014.

claim: An aromatic side chain located at the entrance of the acidic pocket, F352 in human ASIC1a (F350 in mouse ASIC1a), plays an important role in PcTx1 activity.
source: An aromatic side chain located at the entrance of the acidic pocket, F352 in human ASIC1a (F350 in mouse ASIC1a), plays an important role in PcTx1 activity because mutations to either alanine or leucine (or ASIC isoforms that naturally carry these residues at this position) display significantly attenuated PcTx1 sensitivity (Sherwood et al., 2009; Sherwood et al., 2011; Saez et al., 2015; Joeres et al., 2016; Cristofori-Armstrong et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutations of F352/F350 to either alanine or leucine display significantly attenuated PcTx1 sensitivity.
source: An aromatic side chain located at the entrance of the acidic pocket, F352 in human ASIC1a (F350 in mouse ASIC1a), plays an important role in PcTx1 activity because mutations to either alanine or leucine (or ASIC isoforms that naturally carry these residues at this position) display significantly attenuated PcTx1 sensitivity (Sherwood et al., 2009; Sherwood et al., 2011; Saez et al., 2015; Joeres et al., 2016; Cristofori-Armstrong et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Species- and state-dependent factors greatly influence the functional outcome of PcTx1 modulation.
source: Additional species- and state-dependent factors greatly influence the functional outcome of PcTx1 modulation (Sherwood et al., 2011; Cristofori-Armstrong et al., 2019), but fundamental mechanistic aspects of this interaction remain unresolved.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sherwood et al., 2011 and Cristofori-Armstrong et al., 2019.

claim: Long-lived conformational changes induced by PcTx1 could affect the activity of endogenous ASIC1a modulators.
source: This is relevant since long-lived conformational changes could affect the activity of endogenous ASIC1a modulators.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about potential implications of the observed conformational changes.

claim: Increased BigDyn levels have been linked to acidosis-induced neuronal cell death.
source: And since increased BigDyn levels have been linked to acidosis-induced neuronal cell death (Sherwood and Askwith, 2009), this long-lasting interference of the 'ECDonly' conformation on the ASIC–BigDyn interaction could contribute to neuroprotective effects and provide a conceptually new route for ASIC-targeting therapeutics.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sherwood and Askwith, 2009.

claim: The long-lasting interference of the 'ECDonly' conformation on the ASIC–BigDyn interaction could contribute to neuroprotective effects.
source: And since increased BigDyn levels have been linked to acidosis-induced neuronal cell death (Sherwood and Askwith, 2009), this long-lasting interference of the 'ECDonly' conformation on the ASIC–BigDyn interaction could contribute to neuroprotective effects and provide a conceptually new route for ASIC-targeting therapeutics.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about potential therapeutic implications.

claim: Functionally silent states and conformations have previously been suggested to occur in other ligand-gated ion channels.
source: Interestingly, such functionally silent states and conformations have previously been suggested to occur also in other ligand-gated ion channels (Dahan et al., 2004; Pless et al., 2007; Pless and Lynch, 2009; Munro et al., 2019) and could, at least in theory, be used to modulate protein–ligand and protein–protein interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Long-lasting conformational changes could interfere with recently proposed metabotropic functions of ASIC1a by altering intracellular protein–protein interactions.
source: We further speculate that long-lasting conformational changes could also interfere with recently proposed metabotropic functions of ASIC1a by altering intracellular protein–protein interactions (Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020), although this will require additional verification.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about potential effects on metabotropic functions.

claim: Reduced PcTx1 inhibition in F350L could, in part, result from the reduced pH sensitivity of the F350L variant.
source: Reduced PcTx1 inhibition could, in part, result from the reduced pH sensitivity of the F350L variant, in line with the critical role of pH on PcTx1 modulation observed for human and rat ASIC1a (Cristofori-Armstrong et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and supported by citation to Cristofori-Armstrong et al., 2019.

claim: PcTx1 still binds to F352L hASIC1a as pre-incubation with PcTx1 prevented the modulatory effects of BigDyn.
